Suggest charts for a data frame

pv_suggest.Rd

The blank-page killer: hand pv_suggest() a data frame and it prints a short list of runnable chart calls with the real column names filled in, each with one line of reasoning. Copy the call you like, run it, and go from there.

Usage

pv_suggest(data, n = 4)

Arguments

data

A data frame to inspect.

n

Maximum number of suggestions to keep, best fit first (default 4).

Value

An object of class pv_suggestions: a list with the data frame's name and dimensions plus a suggestions list, one record per suggestion with chart (the function's name), code (the runnable call, sometimes led by an aggregate() line), and reason (one plain-English line). Its print method renders the numbered list; the object itself is returned for programmatic use.

Details

The suggestions come from what is actually in the data: column types and cardinalities, whether keys repeat (which decides between a direct call and an aggregate() step, printed as part of the code), a Date or year column (lines; a calendar for daily dates; a slope chart when it holds exactly two moments per group; a horizon chart when a grouping holds more series than the palette has colours, the point where a line chart turns to spaghetti), pairs of numeric columns (scatter, with density = TRUE past a few thousand rows and the reason naming density = "hex" as the countable alternative; a dumbbell when exactly two share a scale with one row per category; a pyramid when exactly two are non-negative and named as opposing flows - in and out, male and female, imports and exports), many numeric columns (a pairs matrix), longitude/latitude pairs (a bubble map), id columns matching the bundled Swiss map layers (a choropleth), a column of two-letter canton codes with one row per canton (a hex cartogram), two place-name columns whose values are feature names on one bundled layer plus a non-negative measure (a flow map), grouped numeric columns (boxplot, violin, or ridgeline, by group count), a signed measure whose losses are a real minority (a waterfall, offered as a guess), nested category columns (a sunburst, with the icicle named as its readable-label twin), and parts of a whole (a donut, with a waffle beside it as the precise-reading alternative). Every candidate is built once behind the scenes before it is offered, so a printed suggestion never errors on the data it was suggested for.

Examples

# Daily weather readings: a calendar and a line top the list.
pv_suggest(pv_weather)
#> <pv_suggestions> pv_weather: 2,192 rows, 6 columns
#> 
#> 1) pv_calendar - `date` is daily, so `temp_mean` reads as a year-at-a-glance calendar - weekday rhythm and seasons jump out
#>    pv_calendar(pv_weather, date = "date", value = "temp_mean")
#> 
#> 2) pv_line - `temp_mean` over `date` reads naturally as a line
#>    pv_line(pv_weather, x = "date", y = "temp_mean")
#> 
#> 3) pv_pairs - 5 numeric columns pair up in one matrix - every relationship and distribution at a glance
#>    pv_pairs(pv_weather, columns = c("temp_mean", "temp_max", "temp_min", "precip_mm", "sunshine_min"))
#> 
#> 4) pv_scatter - two numeric columns invite a look at how `temp_max` moves with `temp_mean`
#>    pv_scatter(pv_weather, x = "temp_mean", y = "temp_max")
#> 

# A date, two categories and two measures - note the aggregate() step
# spelled out where a chart needs one row per key.
pv_suggest(pv_sales)
#> <pv_suggestions> pv_sales: 480 rows, 6 columns
#> 
#> 1) pv_horizon - 24 `month` series would tangle as spaghetti lines; the horizon folds each into its own compact shaded ribbon (summed to one row per `date`/`month` first)
#>    by_date_month <- aggregate(units ~ date + month, pv_sales, sum)
#>    pv_horizon(by_date_month, x = "date", y = "units", series = "month")
#> 
#> 2) pv_line - a date and a numeric per region read naturally as lines (summed to one row per `date`/`region` first)
#>    by_date_region <- aggregate(units ~ date + region, pv_sales, sum)
#>    pv_line(by_date_region, x = "date", y = "units", series = "region")
#> 
#> 3) pv_heatmap - one value per `product`/`region` pair reads as a colour grid - patterns across the whole matrix at once (summed to one row per `product`/`region` first)
#>    by_product_region <- aggregate(units ~ product + region, pv_sales, sum)
#>    pv_heatmap(by_product_region, x = "product", y = "region", value = "units")
#> 
#> 4) pv_scatter - two numeric columns invite a look at how `revenue` moves with `units`
#>    pv_scatter(pv_sales, x = "units", y = "revenue")
#> 

# Municipality ids that match the bundled Lucerne map layer.
fiscal25 <- subset(pv_fiscal, year == 2025)
pv_suggest(fiscal25)
#> <pv_suggestions> fiscal25: 79 rows, 6 columns
#> 
#> 1) pv_choropleth - the ids in `municipality_id` are Lucerne municipality numbers, so `resource_per_capita` can be painted by region
#>    pv_choropleth(fiscal25, id = "municipality_id", value = "resource_per_capita")
#> 
#> 2) pv_scatter - two numeric columns invite a look at how `resource_index` moves with `resource_per_capita`
#>    pv_scatter(fiscal25, x = "resource_per_capita", y = "resource_index", label = "municipality")
#> 
#> 3) pv_histogram - the spread of `resource_per_capita` is worth a first look on its own
#>    pv_histogram(fiscal25, x = "resource_per_capita")
#> 
#> 4) pv_table - a sortable table shows the raw rows while you decide
#>    pv_table(fiscal25)
#> 

# Exactly two census years per city: the slope chart's home ground.
census <- subset(pv_city_population, year %in% c(1930, 2024))
pv_suggest(census)
#> <pv_suggestions> census: 358 rows, 4 columns
#> 
#> 1) pv_slope - `year` holds exactly two years (1930 and 2024), so each `city` draws one line whose slope is its change
#>    pv_slope(census, x = "year", y = "population", group = "city")
#> 
#> 2) pv_bar - one number per `size_class` compares cleanly as bars (summed to one row per `size_class` first)
#>    by_size_class <- aggregate(population ~ size_class, census, sum)
#>    pv_bar(by_size_class, x = "size_class", y = "population")
#> 
#> 3) pv_boxplot - `population` repeats across 6 `size_class` groups; boxes compare the spreads
#>    pv_boxplot(census, value = "population", group = "size_class")
#> 
#> 4) pv_histogram - the spread of `population` is worth a first look on its own
#>    pv_histogram(census, x = "population")
#> 

# 26 cantons over 21 years - past the spaghetti threshold, so a
# horizon chart is offered where a line chart would drown.
pv_suggest(pv_tourism)
#> <pv_suggestions> pv_tourism: 6,006 rows, 6 columns
#> 
#> 1) pv_choropleth - the ids in `canton_id` are canton numbers, so `arrivals` can be painted by region (summed to one row per `canton_id` first)
#>    by_canton_id <- aggregate(arrivals ~ canton_id, pv_tourism, sum)
#>    pv_choropleth(by_canton_id, map = "cantons", id = "canton_id", value = "arrivals")
#> 
#> 2) pv_horizon - 26 `canton` series would tangle as spaghetti lines; the horizon folds each into its own compact shaded ribbon (summed to one row per `year`/`canton` first)
#>    by_year_canton <- aggregate(arrivals ~ year + canton, pv_tourism, sum)
#>    pv_horizon(by_year_canton, x = "year", y = "arrivals", series = "canton")
#> 
#> 3) pv_line - a year and a numeric per origin read naturally as lines (summed to one row per `year`/`origin` first)
#>    by_year_origin <- aggregate(arrivals ~ year + origin, pv_tourism, sum)
#>    pv_line(by_year_origin, x = "year", y = "arrivals", series = "origin")
#> 
#> 4) pv_heatmap - one value per `canton`/`origin` pair reads as a colour grid - patterns across the whole matrix at once (summed to one row per `canton`/`origin` first)
#>    by_canton_origin <- aggregate(arrivals ~ canton + origin, pv_tourism, sum)
#>    pv_heatmap(by_canton_origin, x = "canton", y = "origin", value = "arrivals")
#> 

# Two columns of canton names and a count: origin-destination flows.
pendler <- data.frame(
  from = c("Aargau", "Luzern", "Schwyz", "Zug"),
  to = c("Zug", "Zug", "Zug", "Luzern"),
  commuters = c(4905, 11251, 4576, 4925))
pv_suggest(pendler)
#> <pv_suggestions> pendler: 4 rows, 3 columns
#> 
#> 1) pv_flow_map - `from` and `to` hold canton names, so each row draws as a curved band from origin to destination
#>    pv_flow_map(pendler, from = "from", to = "to", value = "commuters")
#> 
#> 2) pv_heatmap - one value per `from`/`to` pair reads as a colour grid - patterns across the whole matrix at once
#>    pv_heatmap(pendler, x = "from", y = "to", value = "commuters")
#> 
#> 3) pv_sunburst - every `from` belongs to exactly one `to`, so `commuters` nests as rings - pv_icicle draws the same tree with readable labels
#>    pv_sunburst(pendler, levels = c("to", "from"), value = "commuters")
#> 
#> 4) pv_bar - one number per `from` compares cleanly as bars
#>    pv_bar(pendler, x = "from", y = "commuters")
#>
